title: Time, phone numbers and age
titleJp: いま なんじですか
canDo: I can ask and tell the time (いま なんじですか。), including "half past" and a.m./p.m.
I can say and understand a phone number in Japanese, digit by digit.
I can say my age and ask someone else's, getting いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい and はたち right.
I can say what year of school or college I'm in (〜ねんせい) and ask なんねんせいですか。

skills: Counting from 0 to 100 without looking (lesson 00-3): this lesson uses those numbers all the time.
Building X は Y です and questions with か and なんですか (lesson 01-1).
Reading hiragana, even slowly. ゼロ and foreign names are in katakana, always with the reading shown.

grammar.title: 〜じ · 〜じはん · いま なんじですか
grammar.explanation:
To tell the time, attach the number to **じ** ("o'clock"): さんじ = 3:00. For "half past", put **はん** right after it: さんじはん = 3:30. It's the same kind of sentence as in lesson 01-1: the time is the **PREDICATE**, with です at the end.
• The question: いま なんじですか。 なんじ ("what time") sits exactly where the answer will go: いま くじです。 Time words like いま ("now") take **no particle** (more on this in lesson 03-3).
• Three hours have special readings: **よじ** (4:00), **しちじ** (7:00) and **くじ** (9:00). The others follow the numbers you already know: いちじ, にじ, さんじ, ごじ, ろくじ, はちじ, じゅうじ, じゅういちじ, じゅうにじ.
• A.m. and p.m. come **before** the time: ごぜん くじ (9 a.m.), ごご さんじ (3 p.m.). ごご covers everything after noon, including the evening. In conversation people usually use the 12-hour clock, adding ごぜん/ごご when it needs to be clear.
grammar.structure: いま [number]じ(はん)です。 · いま なんじですか。 · ごぜん / ごご + [time]

examples.jp: いま なんじですか。— くじはんです。
examples.kana: いま なんじですか。— くじはんです。
examples.romaji: Ima nanji desu ka. — Kuji han desu.
examples.en: What time is it now? — It's 9:30.

examples.jp: サンパウロは いま ごご しちじです。とうきょうは ごぜん しちじです。
examples.kana: サンパウロは いま ごご しちじです。とうきょうは ごぜん しちじです。
examples.romaji: Sanpauro wa ima gogo shichiji desu. Tōkyō wa gozen shichiji desu.
examples.en: In São Paulo it's 7 p.m. now. In Tokyo it's 7 a.m. [lit. as for São Paulo, now p.m. 7 o'clock is]

examples.jp: いま よじですか。— いいえ、よじはんです。
examples.kana: いま よじですか。— いいえ、よじはんです。
examples.romaji: Ima yoji desu ka. — Iie, yoji han desu.

pitfalls: 4:00 is よじ and 9:00 is くじ: よんじ ✗ → よじ ✓; きゅうじ ✗ → くじ ✓. 7:00 is しちじ (you'll sometimes hear ななじ, but the standard form, and Genki's, is しちじ).
はん comes right after じ: はんくじ ✗, くじと はん ✗ → くじはん ✓ ("half past nine").
ごぜん and ごご come before the time, the opposite of English "3 p.m.": さんじ ごご ✗ → ごご さんじ ✓.
じ is a time on the clock, not a length of time: にじ = "2 o'clock". "For two hours" is にじ ✗ → にじかん ✓ (lesson 04-3).
howToStudy: Today, every time you look at a clock, say the time out loud, rounded to the hour or the half hour: いま にじはんです。

Tap 🔬 on example 2: サンパウロは is the TOPIC, いま and ごご show up as TIME, and しちじです is the PREDICATE. Then say the sentence in English starting from the predicate: "it's 7… p.m.… now… as for São Paulo". (The two cities are 12 hours apart, which is why both say しちじ.)
In your notebook, write 1:00 to 12:00 in kana and circle the three special ones: よじ, しちじ, くじ.

grammar.title: Phone numbers
grammar.gloss: digit by digit, with の between the groups
grammar.explanation:
A phone number is read **digit by digit**, never as one big number: 080 is ゼロはちゼロ, not "eighty". Where the hyphen is, between one group and the next, you say **の** (with a small pause). Zero is **ゼロ** or **れい**; in speech, ゼロ is more common.
• To avoid confusion, use **よん** (4), **なな** (7) and **きゅう** (9), not し, しち, く: on the phone, し, しち and いち are easy to mix up.
• In speech, many Japanese speakers stretch 2 and 5 (にい, ごお) to keep the rhythm even. It's optional: に and ご are correct.
• The question follows the pattern from lesson 01-1: でんわばんごうは なんですか。 The answer is the PREDICATE: [number] です。
• The same rule works for numbers from any country, like the Brazilian number in example 3.
• In Japan, cell phone numbers usually start with 090, 080 or 070. In writing, people use digits; the kana readings in this lesson are there so you can practice the pronunciation.
grammar.structure: [group] の [group] の [group] です。 · でんわばんごうは なんですか。

examples.jp: でんわばんごうは なんですか。— ゼロはちゼロの よんろくいちにの さんななはちごです。
examples.kana: でんわばんごうは なんですか。— ゼロはちゼロの よんろくいちにの さんななはちごです。
examples.romaji: Denwa bangō wa nan desu ka. — Zero-hachi-zero no yon-roku-ichi-ni no san-nana-hachi-go desu.

examples.jp: だいがくの でんわばんごうは れいろくの ごにきゅうはちの いちななよんれいです。
examples.kana: だいがくの でんわばんごうは れいろくの ごにきゅうはちの いちななよんれいです。
examples.romaji: Daigaku no denwa bangō wa rei-roku no go-ni-kyū-hachi no ichi-nana-yon-rei desu.

examples.jp: ルーカスさんの でんわばんごうは いちいちの きゅうごさんにいちの はちななろくよんです。
examples.kana: ルーカスさんの でんわばんごうは いちいちの きゅうごさんにいちの はちななろくよんです。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu-san no denwa bangō wa ichi-ichi no kyū-go-san-ni-ichi no hachi-nana-roku-yon desu.

pitfalls: Don't read the groups as big numbers: 4612 is よんろくいちに, not "four thousand six hundred twelve".
The hyphen becomes の: ゼロはちゼロの よんろくいちにの…. Don't say "hyphen". (In speech you'll sometimes hear just a pause instead of の; use の, which is Genki's standard.)
English speakers often say "oh" for zero ("oh-eight-oh"). In Japanese, zero is ゼロ or れい, never お: おはちお ✗ → ゼロはちゼロ ✓.
On the phone, prefer よん, なな and きゅう. Saying し (4) or しち (7) inside a number is asking to be misheard.
howToStudy: Say your cell number in Japanese 3 times out loud, with の between the groups. Then say the numbers of 2 people in your contacts.
Tap 🔊 on example 1 and repeat along, pausing at each の.
Out and about or online, read 3 numbers you see (a phone number in an ad, a bus number) in Japanese, digit by digit.

grammar.title: 〜さい · なんさい
grammar.explanation:
Age = number + **さい**, in an X は Y です sentence: すずきさんは にじゅうごさいです。 ("Mr./Ms. Suzuki is 25.") The age is the PREDICATE, with です at the end, and さい already means "years old". The question is **なんさいですか**, with なんさい exactly where the answer goes.
• **Sound changes**: **いっさい** (1), **はっさい** (8), **じゅっさい** (10). They stay inside bigger numbers: じゅういっさい (11), じゅうはっさい (18), よんじゅういっさい (41). You may also hear じっさい for 10.
• 20 has its own word: **はたち**, without さい. (にじゅっさい exists, but はたち is the usual word.) From 21 on, everything follows the pattern again: にじゅういっさい, にじゅうにさい….
• The others are regular: よんさい (4), ななさい (7), きゅうさい (9).
• With older people or in formal situations, the more polite question is おいくつですか。
grammar.structure: [person] は [number] さいです。 · なんさいですか。

examples.jp: ルーカスさんは なんさいですか。— じゅうはっさいです。
examples.kana: ルーカスさんは なんさいですか。— じゅうはっさいです。
examples.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa nansai desu ka. — Jūhassai desu.

examples.jp: わたしは はたちです。りゅうがくせいです。
examples.kana: わたしは はたちです。りゅうがくせいです。
examples.romaji: Watashi wa hatachi desu. Ryūgakusei desu.

examples.jp: わたしの ねこは いっさいです。
examples.kana: わたしの ねこは いっさいです。
examples.romaji: Watashi no neko wa issai desu.
examples.en: My cat is one year old.

pitfalls: English puts "how old" at the start of the question. In Japanese, なんさい stays where the answer will go, right before です: なんさい ルーカスさんは ですか ✗ → ルーカスさんは なんさいですか ✓.
はたち is already the whole age: はたちさい ✗ → はたちです ✓.
1, 8 and 10 change sound: いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい (or じっさい). いちさい ✗ and じゅうさい ✗. You'll also hear はちさい in speech, but the standard form, and Genki's, is はっさい.
With older people, prefer おいくつですか to なんさいですか, and don't ask someone's age right away.
howToStudy: Say out loud the ages of 5 friends or relatives: (name)さんは 〜さいです。 If you can, include someone who is 18, 20 or 21.
Tap 🔬 on example 1: ルーカスさんは is the TOPIC and なんさいですか is the PREDICATE. In the answer, じゅうはっさいです takes the same place.
In your notebook, write the ages from 1 to 10 in kana and circle the ones that change sound.

grammar.title: 〜ねんせい · なんねんせい
grammar.explanation:
To say what year you're in at school or college, use number + **ねんせい**: にねんせい = a second-year student. The question: **なんねんせいですか**. There are no special words like "freshman" or "sophomore": you just count the year.
• Watch the 4: **よねんせい**, not よんねんせい.
• To say where, use the の from lesson 01-1: だいがくの さんねんせい ("a third-year at college"), こうこうの いちねんせい ("a first-year in high school", roughly a 10th grader in the US). The block with の **describes** the next one, and ねんせい is the core.
• ねんせい is your **school year**, not your age. For age, use さい.
• In Japan, college usually lasts 4 years and high school (こうこう) 3.
grammar.structure: [person] は ([school] の) [number] ねんせいです。 · なんねんせいですか。

examples.jp: アナさんは なんねんせいですか。— よねんせいです。
examples.kana: アナさんは なんねんせいですか。— よねんせいです。
examples.romaji: Ana-san wa nannensei desu ka. — Yonensei desu.
examples.en: What year is Ana in? — She's in her fourth year.

examples.jp: わたしは だいがくの にねんせいです。
examples.kana: わたしは だいがくの にねんせいです。
examples.romaji: Watashi wa daigaku no ninensei desu.
examples.en: I'm a second-year student at college. [lit. as for me, college's second-year student is]

examples.jp: やまださんは こうこうの さんねんせいです。じゅうはっさいです。
examples.kana: やまださんは こうこうの さんねんせいです。じゅうはっさいです。
examples.romaji: Yamada-san wa kōkō no sannensei desu. Jūhassai desu.
examples.en: Yamada is a third-year high school student, 18 years old.

pitfalls: The 4th year is よねんせい: よんねんせい ✗ → よねんせい ✓.
The order is the reverse of English "of": "second year of college" is だいがくの にねんせい ✓. にねんせいの だいがく ✗ would be "the second-year's college".
ねんせい is only for students. People who work say what they do (かいしゃいんです) or their age.
Don't mix up school year and age: "I'm 2 years old" is にさいです; にねんせいです is "I'm in my second year".
howToStudy: Say out loud what year you're in, or imagine you're studying in Japan: だいがくの 〜ねんせいです。
Build example 3 from the end, out loud: さんねんせいです → こうこうの さんねんせいです → やまださんは こうこうの さんねんせいです。 Then tap 🔬 on it: こうこうの shows up as DESCRIBES NEXT, attached to さんねんせいです (the PREDICATE).
Combine lesson 01-1 and this one into a 30-second introduction (name → nationality → age → year) and record it on your phone.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook, writing the Japanese in kana. Spell the numbers out in kana to practice reading them. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day.

tasks.prompt: Write each time in kana, the way you would say it.

items.note: Special: よじ, never よんじ.
ごぜん goes first, and 9:00 is くじ.
ごご goes before the time, the opposite of English "3 p.m.".

a.jp: いま なんじですか。— いちじはんです。
a.romaji: Ima nanji desu ka. — Ichiji han desu.

tasks.prompt: Write in kana how you would read each phone number, with の between the groups.

a.jp: ゼロきゅうゼロの にななろくさんの ごいちはちよん
ゼロさんの よんはちにきゅうの いちゼロごなな

items.note: れい instead of ゼロ is also correct.

a.jp: ゼロななゼロの きゅうさんいちろくの よんよんゼロに

items.note: On the phone, 7 is なな and 4 is よん.

a.jp: ともだちの アナさんは はたちです。
a.romaji: Tomodachi no Ana-san wa hatachi desu.

items.note: No さい: はたち is the whole age. ともだちの describes アナさん ("my friend Ana").

a.jp: ペドロさんの ねこは じゅっさいです。
a.romaji: Pedoro-san no neko wa jussai desu.

items.note: 10 years old = じゅっさい (or じっさい).

a.jp: すずきさんは よんじゅういっさいです。

items.note: 41 = よんじゅう + いっさい: the sound change of 1 still applies.

a.jp: なんさいですか。— じゅうきゅうさいです。

items.note: No あなた, as in lesson 01-1. おいくつですか。 (more polite) is also correct.

a.jp: だいがくの いちねんせいです。

items.note: Starting with わたしは is also correct.

items.q: What year is Lucas in? — Fourth year.

a.jp: ルーカスさんは なんねんせいですか。— よねんせいです。
a.romaji: Rūkasu-san wa nannensei desu ka. — Yonensei desu.

items.note: よねんせい, with no ん.

tasks.prompt: Write a mini profile of yourself in 5 sentences: your name, your age, your year at school or college (or what you do), a made-up phone number and what time it is now. Then read it aloud and record it on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: わたしの なまえは アナです。はたちです。だいがくの にねんせいです。でんわばんごうは ゼロはちゼロの いちにさんよんの ごろくななはちです。いま ごご さんじはんです。
a.romaji: Watashi no namae wa Ana desu. Hatachi desu. Daigaku no ninensei desu. Denwa bangō wa zero-hachi-zero no ichi-ni-san-yon no go-roku-nana-hachi desu. Ima gogo sanji han desu.
a.en: My name is Ana. I'm 20. I'm a second-year college student. My phone number is 080-1234-5678. It's 3:30 p.m. now.

items.note: Check: よじ/しちじ/くじ if they come up, はたち without さい, いっさい/はっさい/じゅっさい, よねんせい, and の between the phone groups and between だいがく and ねんせい.

practice.what: Play normally and hunt for numbers: whenever a number appears on screen or in a dialogue, read it aloud in Japanese. If a line of dialogue has なんじ, 〜じ, 〜さい or 〜ねんせい, pause and copy it into your notebook.
Drills → Numbers: 10 min. Then the Lesson 1 vocabulary in the SRS.
Practice L1: listening and comprehension, to hear numbers and times inside sentences.
Tap 🔊 on the phone and age examples and repeat along 3 times, pausing at each の.
Record yourself in 30 seconds or less: いま 〜じです。 + your age + your year (or what you do). Listen back and check the special readings.

culture.title: The Japanese school year starts in April
culture.body: In Japan, the school year **starts in April** and ends in March, rather than starting around September as in the US and much of Europe. New students are welcomed with an entrance ceremony, the にゅうがくしき, which in many regions falls around cherry-blossom season. So a student who is an いちねんせい in March becomes a にねんせい in April, not at the start of the calendar year. School grades are grouped by birth date, from April 2 to April 1 of the following year: a child born in March is in the same grade as children born the April before. The government and many companies also start their fiscal year in April, and new employees usually start work that month.
culture.try: Think of two children born in the same year, one in March and one in May. Would they be in the same grade in Japan? (No: the one born in March starts school a year earlier.) Then say your own year out loud, the Japanese way: だいがくの 〜ねんせいです。, or, if you've already graduated, your age: 〜さいです。

checklist: I can say the times from 1:00 to 12:00, with and without はん, without looking, getting よじ, しちじ and くじ right.
I can ask いま なんじですか。 and understand the answer, with ごぜん and ごご before the time.
I can say my phone number in Japanese, digit by digit, with の between the groups.
I can say my age and ask なんさいですか。 without mixing up いっさい, はっさい, じゅっさい and はたち.
I can say what year I'm in (〜ねんせい) and I remember that the 4th is よねんせい.
